analysis.title: Down but not out
key_insights: Copper fell sharply toward USD 12,000/mt (spot 12,251 on 20 Nov 2026), contrary to UBS's expectation that prices would stay well supported. Demand worries are the main driver.

Sentiment hit by uncertainty over AI and data center investment, and by China's October data, which disappointed on consumer spending and fixed-asset investment. LME copper inventories are also rising.

COMEX-LME arbitrage spread turned negative at about USD -350/mt, versus roughly +USD 5 to +150/mt in October. The October positive spread had pulled copper into the US ahead of potential Section 232 tariffs.
UBS cut its March 2027 forecast to USD 14,500/mt from USD 15,000/mt. June and September 2027 stay at USD 15,500/mt, and a new end-December 2027 forecast of USD 15,500/mt was introduced.

UBS expects market deficits of about 219,000 mt in 2026 and 379,000 mt in 2027 and favors long copper positions. As an alternative it favors selling downside volatility to earn yield while keeping exposure to downside price risk.

Mine supply growth is constrained, particularly in Chile. Antofagasta lowered copper guidance, First Quantum narrowed its full-year outlook and BHP reported lower y/y output. Teck's output was stronger and partly offsets this.

Spot treatment and refining charges (TCRCs) in China remain deeply depressed because of concentrate shortages. China's refined copper output has moderated on smelter maintenance and lower operating rates. It is unclear whether cuts extend into 2027 or are temporary ahead of the 2027 TCRC negotiations.

China's physical market is tight. Shanghai inventories are near multi-year lows, and the Yangshan cathode premium over LME spot rose from about USD 120/mt in October to a record USD 500/mt in November.
Global manufacturing PMI eased to 52.6 in October from 53 in September, still above 50. Input-price inflation accelerated and delivery times lengthened.
Elevated prices and physical premiums are weighing on midstream demand (wire, cable, rod) and discouraging restocking. Electrification, grid investment, renewables and EVs continue to support demand.
China demand is subdued: fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% y/y in January-October, new construction starts fell about 24.4% and completions 26.6% y/y, and October retail spending grew 0.4%.
China's October imports of unwrought copper and products fell about 1.5% m/m to 450,000 mt (+2.3% y/y). January-October imports fell 6% to 4.21 million mt, partly on weak smelter economics.
Main upside risk to available supply is a release of elevated US copper inventories if the US administration does not proceed with copper import tariffs.

LME net-long positioning fell by about 22,500 contracts from October to 20,915 contracts in November, and prices are oversold. Technical support sits at USD 11,650/mt and USD 10,900/mt. UBS sees the correction stabilizing if supply constraints persist and global growth is 3.5% in 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Mine supply growth is constrained in Chile, China TCRCs are deeply depressed, Shanghai inventories are near multi-year lows, and UBS forecasts deficits of 219,000 mt in 2026 and 379,000 mt in 2027. Positioning is less stretched and prices are oversold.
tension_points.bear_case: Weak China demand, rising LME inventories, uncertainty over AI and data center investment, a negative COMEX-LME spread, high prices discouraging restocking, and possible release of US inventories if tariffs are not imposed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A break below technical support at USD 11,650/mt and then USD 10,900/mt, or US copper inventories being released if tariffs are not imposed.

theme_stances.key_argument: Constrained mine supply and forecast deficits support a copper recovery in 2027 despite the demand-driven pullback.
theme_stances.evidence: we retain a positive outlook for copper prices
